title: Engineering AI Discover
summary:
The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer

By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi

We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.

Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.

This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.

Why an intelligence layer?

Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.

The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:

  1. Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.
  2. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.
  3. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.
  4. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.
  5. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.
  6. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.
  7. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.

System Architecture

When a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.

The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.

A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.

Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.

The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.

Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.

Key Decisions

Each challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.

1. Design the product and architecture around LLMs

We reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.

This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.

2. Make existing systems composable

Keeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.

Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.

In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.

3. Plan first, then execute

To contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.

Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.

This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.

4. Stay model and capability agnostic

The best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.

That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.

Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.

Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.

5. Make page generation asynchronous

Inference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.

Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.

Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.

6. Enforce safety in code

Some rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.

For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.

Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.

Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.

7. Remember what members tell us

A taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.

In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.

The member holds the remote

In this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.

  • The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.
  • Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.

What’s next

It would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.

We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:

  • How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.
  • What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.

Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.

This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.

Acknowledgements

We would like to thank Adi Suresh, Akash Katipally, Allan Johns, Becks Wood, Bhargav Mangipudi, Carrie Santiago, Chris Martin, Claire Campbell, Corey Waldin, Dana Sittler, Daneo Zhang, David Leen, Devon Bryant, Dharamendra Kumar, Dharini Chandrasekaran, Ebony Turner, Federico Roa, Gianfranco Cuoco, Guru Tahasildar, Haley Clanton, Haresh Chudgar, Ivan Provalov, James Schultz, JingXu Yang, Josie Shaw, Kamelia Aryafar, Kate Cummings, Kathleen Garrity, Kelley Robinson, Kevin Du, Kevin O’Connor, Kyla Moore, Kyle Lind, Laura Matsuura, Leah Cusella, Lingyi Liu, Lingyong Wang, Mallory Walkup, Matthew Pereira, Michael Galassi, Minsu Jang, Moumita Bhattacharya, Paran Jain, Paul Lee, Qusai Al-Rabadi, Scarlet Chen, Sergi Perez, Sriram Rao, Stephen Shaw, Sura Elamurugu, Varad Pathak, Yesu Feng, Zainab Mahar Mir, and Zhongli Cheng for their contributions to this work.

title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
summary:
By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein.

Introduction

Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen:

If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode.

A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything.

“In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.”

Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not.

Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize:

  1. High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.
  2. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis.

Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses.

So, what exactly does factuality mean?

Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1:

Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.”

It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show.

Let’s take another example:

Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.”

Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual.

But what about this?

Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.”

Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis?

Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch.

Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:

Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”

Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.

So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?

Current Service and Its Limitations

Our current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:

  1. High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.
  2. Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.

Optimizing the Holistic Pipeline

To understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:

Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?

Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:

  • Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.
  • Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.

This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.

The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.

Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:

Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new information

With confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?

Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specialized

Instead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:

  • Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?
  • Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?

Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.

Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hid

At this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?

Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:

Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:

  • Makes an assumption.
  • Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).
  • Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.

We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:

  1. Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.
  2. Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.

Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality Service

Our findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.

We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:

  • FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.
  • PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.

Results

Based on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:

Evaluation: Datasets and Metrics

We evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.

We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:

Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.

On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.

Evaluation Results

The best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.

Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.

Our takeaways from this experiment are:

  • Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.
  • Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.
  • Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.
  • Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.
  • Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.

Alignment with Human Rationale

So far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?

To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.

We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.

Conclusion + Future Work

Overall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:

  • On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.
  • On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.

The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:

  • Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.
  • Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis.
